32:
If only my ‘was’ turned back to ‘is’,
without waiting for another ‘will be’,
or the time already came
for what will happen afterwards …
34:
At last, as everything passes,
the happiness that Fortune gave me
when she was not ungenerous passed away,
and she never gave it back,
neither in abundance nor in small measures.
For centuries you have seen me now,
Fortune, lying at your feet.
Make me fortunate again,
for my life would be happy
if only my ‘was’ turned back to ‘is’.
35:
I seek no other pleasure or glory,
no other palm or conquest,
no other triumph, no other victory,
only to return to the happiness
whose memory causes me pain.
If you take me back there,
Fortune, all the fierceness
of my burning pain will be tempered,
especially if this happiness comes at once,
without waiting for another ‘will be’.
36:
I ask for impossible things,
for to make time be again
after it has once been
is beyond any power on earth:
none has ever reached so far.
Time runs, flies, and goes
swiftly away, and will not return.
It would be a mistake to ask
that time had already gone,
or the time already came.
37:
I live a life of uncertainty,
now hoping, now fearing.
It is unmistakable death,
and it would be far better to die
and find a way out of pain.
It would be to my advantage
to end my life; yet it is not,
for, on better reflection,
what keeps me alive is fear
for what will happen afterwards.
41:
The lovely maiden breaks through the wall,
she who opened noble Pyramus’s heart.
Love leaves Cyprus and goes straight
to see the narrow, marvellous crack.
Silence speaks there, for the voice dares not
enter through so narrow a passage.
But souls do, for love knows how
to make the hardest thing easy.
Desire exceeded all measure, and the reckless
maiden’s steps seek, for her pleasure,
her own death. See what a story:
at the same instant—oh, strange event!—
both are killed, hidden, and brought back to life
by one sword, one tomb, one memory.
42: ‘Blessed be God,’ said Don Quixote when he had heard Don Lorenzo’s sonnet, ‘that among the countless burned-out poets I have found a consummate poet, which, sir, the artistry of this sonnet shows me you are!’
